blocks.c: I have thought about that a lot since: that the thing which saved me was a habit I had for boring reasons.

I write good logs. I write good logs because my first month here a lift engineer told me that a maintenance log is the only thing in a building that is legally assumed to be true, and if you write it down and date it, you are protected, and if you don't, you're just a guy who says he checked.
So I write everything. Times. Serial numbers. Which tube in which fitting. Weather. I am, by a distance, the most boring employee this building has ever had.
Turns out that is a qualification.
The next night I went to the grey cabinet and took out the 1994 volume, and I read the whole thing, all four hundred pages, on the freight car floor between walks.
It is mostly a maintenance log. Boilers. A leak on 19. A long and increasingly personal war with a pigeon.
And in the margins, in block capitals, in a hand that gets steadier over the year:
MARCH. NEW NIGHT TECH. HE FOUND THE KEY IN WEEK TWO. TOO FAST.
APRIL. TOLD HIM RULE ONE. HE THINKS IT IS A JOKE.
JUNE. HE HAS STOPPED WRITING THINGS DOWN. HE SAYS HE REMEMBERS.
AUGUST. HE WENT DOWN ON THE 14TH. HE HAS NOT COME UP.
SEPTEMBER. I SIGNED HIM OUT MYSELF. IT WOULD NOT ACCEPT IT. IT SAYS ONLY THE PERSON CAN SIGN.
OCTOBER. I AM GOING DOWN AFTER HIM. IF YOU ARE READING THIS, I DID NOT COME UP EITHER, AND YOU SHOULD PUT THIS BOOK BACK.
I did not put the book back.

I turned to the last written page of 1994, and under the pigeon war and the boiler and all of it, there was one final line, in the same capitals, but written with the pen pressed so hard it went through three pages:
MY NAME IS WEN AGUILAR AND I AM ON FLOOR MINUS THREE.
